name: EGCG-glucoside

lead: EGCG-glucoside is a sugar-linked version of green tea's EGCG. It is named as one of two components in the Redensyl hair-growth ingredient.
The only study found on it examined a digestive enzyme in vitro, not hair.

paras: No hair-growth mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
Oral EGCG at high intakes is linked to liver toxicity per EFSA; no safety data for the topical glucoside were found.

studies.title: Inhibitory effects of epigallocatechin gallate and its glucoside on the human intestinal maltase inhibition.

lead: EGCG-glucoside (EGCG2) is a glucosylated form of epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), the main catechin of green tea. In hair-care marketing it is named as one of the two components of Redensyl, alongside dihydroquercetin glucoside.[1]

Published work on EGCG-glucoside is chiefly biochemical. A 2012 in vitro study found that EGCG and its glucoside both inhibited the human intestinal enzyme maltase, with IC50 values of about 20 and 31.5 micromolar respectively.[2] That study concerns diabetes-related enzymes, not hair.

paras: No studies found for EGCG-glucoside alone in hair or any human outcome. A multi-ingredient Redensyl serum has been tested in a small cosmetic study, so effects cannot be assigned to this component.

EGCG is the most abundant catechin in tea and is poorly absorbed orally. Excessive intake has been linked to liver toxicity, and the EFSA stated in 2018 that intakes of 800 mg or more daily could raise liver risk; the FDA has issued warning letters to supplement makers over disease claims.[1] These points concern oral EGCG, not topical cosmetic use.
